passage.bullet: Luther’s 95 arguments attacked friars selling indulgences for Purgatory → challenged papal spiritual authority
Printed copies spread rapidly from Wittenberg across Europe → turned local protest into the Reformation
Henry VIII wrote defending Catholic sacraments → Pope Leo X named him Defender of the Faith

context.bullet: Latin Bibles kept ordinary Christians reliant on priests → Luther’s challenge broke Rome’s monopoly
Moveable-type presses mass-produced cheap pamphlets → prevented Church authorities silencing Luther like earlier critics

stems.stem: In October 1517, German monk ____________ challenged Rome by attacking corrupt friars who sold ____________.
Because ____________ carried Luther’s ideas rapidly across Europe, a single protest in ____________ triggered the Reformation.
Initially, King Henry VIII opposed the Reformation by defending ____________, winning the papal title ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: In 1521 Henry VIII was a devout Catholic defending the Pope against Luther—do not assume Henry backed Protestantism from 1517.

passage.bullet: Catherine of Aragon passed forty with only Princess Mary surviving → left Henry without a son
Lacking a male heir threatened Tudor succession → risked rival nobles plunging England into civil war
Infatuated with Anne Boleyn, Henry cited Leviticus → claimed marrying Catherine was cursed before God

context.bullet: Henry VII won the crown in 1485 after bloody wars → Tudor rule still felt fragile
Catherine had first married Henry’s dead brother Arthur → gave Henry scriptural grounds to challenge validity

stems.stem: Driven by fear of ____________, Henry desperately wanted a ____________ because Catherine had borne only Princess Mary.
Falling deeply in love with ____________ gave Henry an urgent personal motive to replace ____________ as Queen.
Citing a strict warning from the Book of ____________, Henry argued his marriage was cursed and demanded an ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Henry sought an annulment declaring his marriage had never legally existed—do not call it a modern divorce.

passage.bullet: Imperial troops ransacked Rome in May 1527 → trapped Pope Clement VII inside Castel Sant’Angelo
Emperor Charles V was Catherine of Aragon’s nephew → forbade the captive Pope from humiliating her
Clement VII revoked Cardinal Wolsey’s London trial to Rome → stalled Henry’s case and ruined Wolsey

context.bullet: Pope Julius II had approved Henry’s marriage → cancelling it meant admitting earlier papal error
Charles V ruled Spain and the Holy Roman Empire → far outweighed Tudor England’s military power

stems.stem: Although popes usually helped monarchs, Clement VII was held prisoner after imperial troops ransacked ____________ in 1527.
Because Catherine’s powerful nephew ____________ controlled Italy, granting Henry’s annulment risked devastating retaliation.
When the Pope cancelled ____________’s London legatine court, Henry’s legal route through Rome collapsed.

lesson_1.watch_out: Pope Clement VII refused primarily out of fear of Catherine’s nephew Emperor Charles V—not merely strict religious principle.

passage.bullet: Henry threatened heavy fines under ancient treason laws → forced English clergy into complete royal submission
Cromwell’s Reformation Parliament halted annates taxes to Rome → starved the papacy of English church income
1533 Act in Restraint of Appeals banned papal courts → let Archbishop Cranmer crown Anne Boleyn

context.bullet: Binding MPs into passing statute laws gave Henry’s break stronger legal legitimacy than solo royal decrees
Wealthy Tudor MPs already resented Church courts and clerical fees → eagerly backed Cromwell’s anti-papal bills

stems.stem: Guided by lawyer ____________, the Crown threatened ancient treason fines until English bishops accepted royal control.
Through the Reformation Parliament, MPs cut ____________ taxes to Rome and passed the 1533 ____________.
Once appeals to the Pope were outlawed, Archbishop ____________ annulled Henry’s marriage and crowned ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Do not confuse Tudor Chief Minister Thomas Cromwell with his distant relative Oliver Cromwell from the 1640s Civil War.

passage.bullet: 1534 Act of Supremacy named Henry Supreme Head → gave him absolute spiritual rule over England
Compulsory loyalty oaths criminalized dissent → objectors such as Sir Thomas More were executed for treason
Dissolving over 800 monasteries between 1536 and 1540 → flooded Henry’s treasury with vast land wealth

context.bullet: 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace protested monastery closures → Henry crushed 30,000 northern rebels to enforce supremacy
Despite seizing papal power and abbeys, Henry stayed traditional in worship → burned outspoken Protestant reformers

stems.stem: Under the November 1534 ____________, Henry replaced the Pope as ____________ of the Church of England.
Subjects who refused compulsory treason oaths, including ____________, were executed to crush opposition.
Between 1536 and 1540, Cromwell dissolved over ____________ monasteries and sold their estates to ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Breaking with Rome made Henry head of the Church, not a strict Protestant—he kept Latin Mass for most of his reign.

passage.bullet: Catholic Queen Mary I burned nearly 300 Protestants → martyrs left deep anti-Catholic hatred across England
Strict Puritans returned from European exile → demanded purging bishops, Latin prayers, and Catholic ritual
Rival Catholic traditionalists and militant reformers pulled opposite ways → threatened religious civil war in 1558

context.bullet: Edward VI’s radical Protestantism followed by Mary’s Counter-Reformation → exhausted parishes swung repeatedly between faiths
Catholic France and Spain watched closely → harsh anti-Catholic laws risked provoking a foreign crusade

stems.stem: Inheriting the throne in 1558, Elizabeth faced bitter anger after Mary I burned almost ____________ Protestants as ____________.
Simultaneously, strict ____________ returning from European exile pressured Elizabeth to strip away ____________ and bishops.
Caught between loyal Catholics and militant Calvinists, England risked descending into ____________ if Elizabeth chose extremes.

lesson_2.watch_out: Puritans were strict Calvinist Protestants returning from European exile—do not confuse them with Catholic rebels.

passage.bullet: Elizabeth chose Supreme Governor over Supreme Head → calmed moderates uneasy about female spiritual rule
Priests and state officials swore royal allegiance → secured outward obedience across parishes and government
Sacking Catholic bishops who refused the oath → let Elizabeth install loyal moderate Protestant leaders

context.bullet: Unlike Henry VIII’s 1534 treason executions, Elizabeth avoided early martyrdoms → lowered tensions among Catholic gentry
Most ordinary parish clergy swore the 1559 oath → prevented chaotic church closures across rural England

stems.stem: To soothe subjects who believed only Christ or the Pope led the Church, Elizabeth took the title ____________.
Under the 1559 ____________, every priest and public official had to swear loyalty to the Crown.
When Marian bishops refused the oath, Elizabeth replaced them with ____________ without triggering bloody executions.

lesson_2.watch_out: Henry VIII claimed the title Supreme Head in 1534, whereas Elizabeth deliberately chose Supreme Governor in 1559.

passage.bullet: One English Prayer Book governed every parish → replaced Latin services while keeping familiar ceremonial order
Compromise communion wording blended Protestant and Catholic phrasing → allowed moderate believers to worship together
Twelve-pence Sunday fines punished absent recusants without probing private beliefs → preserved peace over persecution

context.bullet: Retaining traditional vestments and church decorations → reassured conservative rural congregations outside Protestant London
Rejecting heresy trials contrasted sharply with Mary I’s burnings → encouraged quiet Catholic conformity

stems.stem: Through the 1559 ____________, every parish used one English Prayer Book with blended ____________ wording.
Catholics known as ____________ who skipped Sunday services paid modest fines rather than facing heresy trials.
Refusing to make ____________ into men’s souls, Elizabeth demanded outward obedience while tolerating quiet private faith.

lesson_2.watch_out: Elizabeth’s Via Media was still an officially Protestant Church—it blended elements for peace, not equal Catholic legal status.

passage.bullet: Northern Earls seized Durham Cathedral in 1569 and restored Catholic Mass → defied Elizabeth’s Settlement
Pope Pius V’s 1570 Regnans in Excelsis excommunicated Elizabeth → commanded Catholics to depose her
Papal absolution freed Catholics from royal oaths → turned peaceful English Catholics into suspected traitors

context.bullet: Mary, Queen of Scots arrived in England in 1568 → gave Catholic rebels a royal figurehead
Regnans in Excelsis arrived after the revolt collapsed → failed to rescue the Northern Earls

stems.stem: Violent resistance erupted in 1569 when traditionalist ____________ marched into Durham Cathedral to restore ____________.
In 1570, Pope Pius V issued ____________, branding Elizabeth a heretic and ordering Catholics to ____________ her.
Because Rome released Catholics from royal allegiance, Elizabeth’s government increasingly viewed every Catholic as a ____________.

lesson_2.watch_out: Pope Pius V’s 1570 bull came too late to help the 1569 Northern Earls—Elizabeth had already crushed their revolt.

passage.bullet: Walsingham’s double agents monitored letters smuggled inside beer barrels → caught Anthony Babington’s assassination plot
Expert cryptographers deciphered Mary Stuart’s secret code → proved she personally endorsed murdering Queen Elizabeth
Armed with undeniable treason evidence, Parliament pressured reluctant Elizabeth → Mary was executed in February 1587

context.bullet: Repeated Ridolfi and Throckmorton plots backed by Spain → convinced councillors Mary was a mortal threat
Executing a crowned queen risked dangerous precedent and foreign outrage → explained Elizabeth’s nineteen-year hesitation

stems.stem: Spymaster Sir Francis ____________ intercepted secret letters smuggled inside ____________ during the 1586 Babington Plot.
Once royal cryptographers cracked her coded reply, ____________ stood convicted of endorsing Elizabeth’s assassination.
Pushed by Parliament, Elizabeth signed the death warrant and Mary was beheaded at ____________ in 1587.

lesson_2.watch_out: Mary, Queen of Scots was Elizabeth’s Catholic cousin Mary Stuart—never confuse her with Elizabeth’s half-sister Queen Mary I.

passage.bullet: Elizabeth sent troops to aid Protestant Dutch rebels → directly undermined Philip II’s rule in Flanders
English privateer Francis Drake plundered Spanish silver ships → crippled Philip’s imperial wealth and pride
Mary Stuart’s 1587 execution won papal blessing → Philip planned ferrying Parma’s army to depose Elizabeth

context.bullet: Once married to Mary I, Philip II lost English influence when Elizabeth rejected his marriage offer
Pope Sixtus V promised financial subsidies once Spanish troops landed → framed invasion as holy war

stems.stem: Outraged by English support for ____________ in the Netherlands and ____________’s raids on Spanish treasure, Philip II prepared war.
Following the 1587 execution of ____________, Philip secured papal blessing for a Catholic crusade against Elizabeth.
Spain’s Armada aimed to command the Channel and escort the ____________’s veteran army across from Flanders.

lesson_3.watch_out: Philip II fought for empire, trade, and Dutch control alongside religion—the Armada was never purely a religious war.

passage.bullet: Drake raided Cadiz harbour in April 1587 and destroyed thirty warships → crippled Spain’s frontline preparations
Burning seasoned barrel wood forced hasty green-wood casks → rotted the Armada’s food and drinking water
Postponing Philip’s invasion until 1588 → gave England twelve vital months to fortify southern coasts

context.bullet: Veteran Admiral Santa Cruz died during the delay → inexperienced nobleman Medina Sidonia inherited command
Extra preparation time let Elizabeth organize hilltop fire beacons and muster county militias across southern England

stems.stem: Sailing boldly into ____________ in April 1587, Francis Drake destroyed thirty warships and delayed Spain’s invasion.
Because Drake burned seasoned ____________, Spanish crews stored provisions in green wood that turned water and bread rotten.
Holding back the Armada for ____________ gave Elizabeth vital time to strengthen English coastal defenses.

lesson_3.watch_out: Burning wooden barrel staves mattered just as much as sinking ships—spoiled water sickened thousands of Spanish sailors in 1588.

passage.bullet: John Hawkins’s sleek race-built galleons outsailed towering Spanish castles → kept English crews beyond grappling range
English ships fired rapid broadsides with long-range brass culverins → battered hulls from safe distance
Medina Sidonia’s tight crescent protected slow transports → prevented heavy Spanish soldiers boarding nimble attackers

context.bullet: Compact four-wheeled English gun carriages reloaded far faster than cumbersome two-wheeled Spanish land mounts
Holding the westerly wind behind them at Plymouth → let Howard and Drake dictate combat distance

stems.stem: While Medina Sidonia’s 130 ships sailed in a defensive ____________, English captains used faster ____________ galleons.
Rather than grappling to board, Howard and Drake fired rapid broadsides from afar using long-range ____________.
Staying deliberately out of reach neutralized Spain’s advantage in heavy ____________ packed aboard floating castles.

lesson_3.watch_out: Channel skirmishes alone did not sink the Armada—Spain’s disciplined crescent formation held firm all the way to Calais.

passage.bullet: Waiting at Calais for Parma’s delayed troops → left Spanish ships crowded in an exposed anchorage
Eight blazing fireships coated in pitch and gunpowder → drifted at midnight into Spain’s anchored fleet
Panicked captains hacked anchor cables to flee → shattered Spain’s protective crescent formation forever

context.bullet: Shallow-water Dutch flyboats blockaded Dunkirk → stopped Parma’s barges ever joining Medina Sidonia’s deep-draught warships
Spanish sailors feared floating gunpowder bombs used earlier at Antwerp → intensified midnight panic at Calais

stems.stem: Anchored off Calais awaiting Parma’s troops, the Spanish panicked when England sent eight blazing ____________ at midnight.
Desperate to escape explosion, Spanish captains ordered crews to cut their ____________ and scatter into the dark.
Breaking their tight ____________ left isolated Spanish galleons vulnerable to close-range English attack.

lesson_3.watch_out: The eight Calais fireships did not burn a single Spanish ship directly—their triumph was panicking captains into breaking formation.

passage.bullet: English warships closed to point-blank range at Gravelines → smashed isolated Spanish hulls and killed hundreds
Fierce gales blocked the Channel return → forced Medina Sidonia’s battered fleet north around Scotland
Ferocious Atlantic storms wrecked anchorless galleons on Irish rocks → barely half the fleet reached Spain

context.bullet: Having cut anchors at Calais → battered Spanish galleons could not hold off jagged Irish cliffs
Elizabeth’s Tilbury speech and Protestant Wind medal → turned survival into lasting proof of God’s favour

stems.stem: Closing to point-blank range at ____________, English guns battered scattered Spanish hulls and drove them into the North Sea.
Forced to sail home around Scotland and ____________, dozens of storm-tossed galleons smashed onto jagged rocks.
After only ____________ damaged ships reached Spain, Elizabeth struck medals proclaiming that God blew and scattered her foes.

lesson_3.watch_out: Weather did not defeat Spain single-handedly—English fireships and gunnery at Gravelines trapped anchorless galleons in the northern storms.

passage.bullet: Claiming Divine Right under God alone, Charles ruled eleven years without MPs → silenced parliamentary criticism
Extending coastal Ship Money to inland counties → let Charles raise permanent revenue without parliamentary consent
John Hampden’s 1637 refusal to pay Ship Money → sparked widespread tax boycotts among propertied gentry

context.bullet: Archbishop Laud imposed ornate altars and ceremonies → convinced Puritan MPs Charles favoured secret popery
Unvoted taxes defied the 1628 Petition of Right → convinced MPs Charles trampled ancient liberties

stems.stem: Convinced by the ____________ of Kings, Charles I dismissed MPs in 1629 and ruled alone for ____________.
Charging ____________ to inland counties outraged landowners because kings traditionally needed Parliament’s vote for taxes.
When ____________ challenged Ship Money in 1637, widespread tax boycotts exposed deep anger toward royal rule.

lesson_4.watch_out: Ruling without calling Parliament was technically legal—MPs called it tyranny because Charles stretched emergency taxes like Ship Money permanently.

passage.bullet: Charles entered the Commons with armed soldiers in January 1642 → shattered parliamentary privilege by force
Warned Five MPs fled by boat into London’s protection → left Charles humiliated before furious citizens
Charles fled London and raised his banner at Nottingham in August 1642 → triggered civil war

context.bullet: Scottish rebellion against Charles’s Prayer Book → bankrupted the Crown and forced Parliament’s recall in 1640
After the Commons raid, MPs distrusted Charles with troops → seized control of England’s militia

stems.stem: Recalled after Scottish rebellion, Parliament broke with Charles when royal guards raided the Commons to arrest ____________.
After his targets escaped by river into the ____________, a humiliated King fled his own capital.
Raising the royal war standard at ____________ in August 1642 turned constitutional deadlock into civil war.

lesson_4.watch_out: No reigning monarch had ever marched armed troops into the House of Commons—that coup destroyed all remaining trust in Charles.

passage.bullet: Parliament’s 1645 New Model Army paid full-time redcoats promoted on merit → outclassed amateur regional militias
Cromwell’s disciplined cavalry crushed royalist flanks at Naseby in June 1645 → routed Charles’s main army
Parliamentary troops seized royal artillery and secret letters → destroyed Charles’s military power and credibility

context.bullet: Unlike Rupert’s Cavaliers chasing plunder, Cromwell’s Ironsides regrouped mid-battle → overwhelmed exposed royalist infantry
Fervent Puritan soldiers sang psalms into battle → believed God backed their fight against royal tyranny

stems.stem: Replacing weak regional militias in 1645, the ____________ promoted full-time soldiers on ____________ rather than noble birth.
Under Fairfax and ____________, disciplined cavalry charges smashed the King’s flanks at the Battle of ____________.
Capturing royal artillery alongside Charles’s private ____________ shattered both his army and his political reputation.

lesson_4.watch_out: Sir Thomas Fairfax was overall Commander-in-Chief of the New Model Army in 1645, while Oliver Cromwell led its cavalry.

passage.bullet: Charles plotted with Scots to restart war → Army leaders branded him a man of blood
Colonel Pride’s troops expelled moderate MPs → left a radical Rump determined to try Charles
Found guilty of treason against his people, Charles was beheaded in 1649 → abolished England’s monarchy

context.bullet: Charles refused to plead at trial → argued no earthly court held lawful power over kings
Treason once meant attacking the King → 1649 judged a monarch guilty of betraying his people

stems.stem: Furious after Charles plotted with Scottish allies to ignite a second war, Army leaders condemned the ____________.
In December 1648, ____________ expelled moderate MPs so a radical ____________ Parliament could create a High Court.
Beheaded outside ____________ on 30 January 1649 for treason against his people, Charles’s death turned England into a ____________.

lesson_4.watch_out: Most elected MPs actually wanted peace talks—regicide happened only after Colonel Pride’s soldiers purged moderates from Parliament.

passage.bullet: William of Orange landed at Torbay in 1688 → Catholic King James II fled to France
Parliament crowned William and Mary on strict terms → ended Stuart claims to unconditional Divine Right
1689 Bill of Rights outlawed unvoted taxes and suspending laws → bound monarchs under Parliament

context.bullet: Birth of James II’s Catholic son in 1688 → raised fears of a permanent Catholic dynasty
Guaranteeing regular Parliaments and free Commons speech → prevented another Eleven Years’ Personal Rule

stems.stem: Alarmed by Catholic King ____________, Protestant nobles invited ____________ to land at Torbay in 1688.
Before crowning William and Mary, MPs required acceptance of the ____________ to bind royal authority.
Henceforth, monarchs could neither cancel ____________ nor collect ____________ without explicit parliamentary consent.

lesson_4.watch_out: The 1689 Bill of Rights limited monarchs rather than creating modern democracy—only wealthy property-owning men could vote for MPs.

passage.bullet: Enacting the Break with Rome via parliamentary statutes → turned MPs into essential lawmaking partners
Ending papal jurisdiction by Act of Parliament → proved King-in-Parliament could reshape even spiritual authority
Selling dissolved monastic estates to local gentry → gave wealthy MPs a permanent stake in reform

context.bullet: Medieval kings mainly summoned MPs for temporary war taxes → Tudor Reformation expanded Parliament’s permanent reach
Meeting across seven years from 1529 → gave the Commons unprecedented confidence and lawmaking experience

stems.stem: Rather than ruling by solo royal decree, Henry VIII used ____________ passed by the Reformation Parliament to break with Rome.
Buying former ____________ estates gave England’s gentry a powerful financial reason to defend ____________.
Using MPs to remake the national Church accidentally laid foundations for future ____________ sovereignty.

lesson_5.watch_out: Henry VIII intended to boost royal power, yet relying on Acts of Parliament inadvertently elevated MPs’ constitutional authority.

passage.bullet: Elizabeth’s 1559 Settlement blended Protestant doctrine with moderate ritual → won broad conformity without heresy trials
Modest Sunday church fines penalized Catholic recusants → maintained parish order while avoiding domestic civil war
Defeating Spain’s 1588 Armada fused patriotism with Protestantism → convinced subjects God protected Elizabeth’s realm

context.bullet: Chains of English Bibles and Protestant martyr stories in parish churches → deepened popular anti-papal identity
Shared dread of Spanish invasion → rallied Elizabethan MPs to fund and defend the Crown

stems.stem: Blending Protestant worship with moderate ceremonies, the 1559 ____________ secured peace through modest ____________ rather than inquisitions.
Crushing the 1588 ____________ forged a powerful patriotic belief that God specially favoured ____________ England.
Shared pride in survival rallied subjects and ____________ closely behind Elizabeth’s Protestant Crown.

lesson_5.watch_out: Anti-Catholic unity forged in 1588 later backfired on Stuart kings whenever MPs suspected the royal court of Catholic sympathies.

passage.bullet: Stuart kings preached Divine Right → claimed monarchs answered only to God, bypassing parliamentary consent
Charles governed eleven years without MPs using unvoted Ship Money → alienated England’s taxpaying gentry
Scots rebelled against forced prayer books → bankrupted Charles into recalling furious MPs in 1640

context.bullet: Decades of Tudor lawmaking had accustomed MPs to partnership → made Stuart absolutism feel unlawful
Ruling England, Presbyterian Scotland, and Catholic Ireland simultaneously → magnified every Stuart religious misstep into crisis

stems.stem: Shattering Tudor partnership, James I and Charles I claimed ____________, insisting monarchs answered to God alone.
During eleven years without MPs, collecting unvoted ____________ convinced landowners that royal power threatened property rights.
Bankrupted when ____________ rebelled against English prayer books, Charles had to summon a hostile Parliament in 1640.

lesson_5.watch_out: Tudor monarchs could also act autocratically, but unlike Charles I they skillfully worked through Parliament instead of lecturing MPs on absolutism.

passage.bullet: Parliament’s citizen army crushed royalist forces at Naseby → shattered the myth of invincible royal authority
Following Pride’s Purge, MPs abolished both monarchy and House of Lords → created a republican Commonwealth
Publicly trying and executing Charles I → proved even anointed monarchs answered to the law

context.bullet: Although monarchy returned in 1660, memory of Whitehall’s scaffold → warned future kings against absolutism
Unlike medieval kings murdered in secret castles, Charles I faced open courtroom prosecution in Westminster Hall

stems.stem: Defeating royalist forces at ____________ and purging Parliament led radicals to abolish monarchy for a ____________.
Putting Charles I on public trial established the revolutionary principle that even an anointed king stood beneath ____________.
Executing a sovereign for ____________ against his own people permanently shattered unquestioned Divine Right.

lesson_5.watch_out: Even though the monarchy was restored in 1660, the 1649 regicide permanently destroyed the idea that kings were untouchable above the law.

passage.bullet: William III and Mary II accepted Parliament’s statutory terms → legally ended absolute Divine Right monarchy
Outlawing unvoted royal taxes and suspending statutes → stripped monarchs of power to govern without MPs
Sovereignty moved from personal royal will to King-in-Parliament → established permanent constitutional monarchy across England

context.bullet: From 1517 papal authority through Tudor supremacy → supreme power finally settled in elected parliamentary statutes
Banning peacetime standing armies without parliamentary consent → forced monarchs to summon MPs every single year

stems.stem: Drafted as a binding legal contract with ____________, the 1689 Bill of Rights ended claims to absolute power.
Monarchs were legally barred from cancelling ____________ or levying ____________ without votes in the Commons.
By 1689, ultimate sovereignty had shifted from the personal will of the Crown to ____________.

lesson_5.watch_out: England became a constitutional monarchy in 1689 rather than a republic—the monarch still reigned, but only through laws passed with Parliament.
